newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk markets calm ahead of treasury debt payments.
newsitem.headline: Turk markets calm ahead of treasury debt payments.

text.p: Bankers said Turkish markets kept calm and rates were subdued ahead of the treasury's heavy domestic debt repayments in coming weeks, but the government's new borrowing requirement would determine the near term trend.
They say the downtrend in interest rates may halt if the treasury increases its borrowing needs to roll-over high debt repayments and finance government spending.

The lira has lost 2.02 percent of its value against the central bank's currency basket of $1 and 1.5 marks so far this month. Bankers expect the lira to depreciate by some 4.5 to 5.5 percent in September, up from four percent in August and 3.5 percent in July.

They think the rise in the lira depreciation is consistent with the pace of monthly inflation which seasonally remains lower in June-August period due to low farm output prices. Markets' expectation for September inflation figure is around 5.5 percent.
"There is no major source of volatility in the foreign exchange market apart from cross foreign exchange rates and some corporate foreign currency demand," said a banker.

Analysts say the central bank is expected to increase cash rates when demand for foreign currency rises. The bank, which holds $16.78 billion of foreign currency in its reserves, may also sell dollars if the lira comes under pressure.
The treasury will service 443 trillion lira of domestic debt by October 9.

Bankers say relatively lower interbank overnight rates, lessened reliance of the treasury on the central bank sources, the government's attempt to issue foreign currency denominated bonds and the treasury's ability to borrow easily are among major reasons behind the mood of financial markets.
The treasury auctioned an unexpectedly high amount of bills worth 102.6 trillion lira this week by raising the average yield 11 points.
Yields on the secondary bond market fell to below 125 percent after the acution.

Overnight cash rates on the central bank-brokered interbank have been running at around 72 percent in the past two weeks. Average overnight rates on the bond market fell to 66 percent this week from 68.55 percent last week. The decline was around six to eight percent in papers with longer maturities.
The treasury has asked banks to submit their bids by Friday's close for three-year foreign currency bonds with an interest of Libor of 260 basis points.
Bankers say the treasury might sell some $750 million to $1 billion worth of bonds.
